plot_extraction.response_text:
Philo Gubb, an eccentric paper-hanger and correspondence-trained detective, uses part of a recent payment to reduce the debt he owes his future father-in-law, who has sold him worthless mining stock. Encouraged by news that his enormously overweight fiancée, Syrilla, is continuing to lose weight and may soon escape her sideshow contract, Gubb returns to his detective work.

He is hired by Dolly O’Hara to find her missing dog, Waffles, which is her chief remembrance of her recently deceased uncle, Haddon O’Hara. At the same time, two rival lawyers offer Gubb separate rewards to locate Mustard Bilton, a missing witness to O’Hara’s baffling will. O’Hara left two nearly identical wills written on opposite sides of the same sheet: one gives the bulk of his estate to Ardelia Doblin, while the other gives it to Sarah Kinsey. Because no one can determine which side was written last, the two women dispute the inheritance, and Mustard may be the only person able to resolve the matter.

Gubb’s microscopic examination of dog hairs and other clues proves useless, so he searches Waffles’s doghouse directly. Inside its roof he finds a hidden envelope from O’Hara giving the dog’s location and instructing that the envelope be delivered to the executor after Waffles is returned. Gubb follows the directions to an abandoned cattle shed, where he finds both Waffles and Mustard. Mustard explains that O’Hara had hired him to steal the dog after his death and wait until Gubb discovered the concealed clue.

Gubb brings Mustard and the envelope to the lawyers, collecting both offered rewards. Mustard reveals that neither side of the double-sided document was O’Hara’s final will. The envelope contains a later, simple will leaving everything to Dolly. O’Hara had arranged the entire mystery—including the conflicting wills, the dog’s disappearance, and Gubb’s investigation—as an elaborate final joke that nevertheless ensures his niece inherits his estate.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a comic detective tale with the atmosphere of early twentieth-century American popular fiction. It combines a small-town legal mystery, a sentimental subplot, and broad character comedy. The central plot imitates the machinery of a conventional detective story—missing persons, microscopic clues, disputed wills, secret documents, and a final revelation—but repeatedly undercuts that machinery through absurdity. The mystery is genuine enough to sustain curiosity, yet its solution depends less on brilliant deduction than on the dead man’s elaborate practical joke and Philo Gubb’s accidental persistence.

The narrator uses a clear, confident third-person voice that is mostly omniscient. It moves freely between present action, explanatory backstory, and concise commentary on characters’ motives and reputations. The narration often maintains a straight face while describing ridiculous circumstances, creating a dry, deadpan effect. Understatement is especially important: assertions such as Gubb’s clues yielding no conclusion “unless the flea in the wool might lead to the conclusion that the dog now, or once, had fleas” parody the solemn logic of detective fiction. The narrator occasionally becomes more openly ironic, as when noting that the inductive method has failed “as it always failed for Mr. Gubb,” but generally lets the disparity between the characters’ seriousness and the absurd facts produce the comedy.

The prose is accessible and energetic, with predominantly medium-length declarative sentences interrupted by longer explanatory passages. Repetition is used for rhythm, emphasis, and comic escalation. The account of O’Hara’s habitual jokes, the duplicated wording of the two wills, and the telegram’s long catalogue of abandoned vegetables all build humor through accumulation. Parallel constructions—“word for word,” “line for line,” and “punctuation mark for punctuation mark”—give the mystery an exaggerated air of exactness. Brief sentences often deliver reversals or punch lines: “But he died. He died and left a will.” The narrative also uses conspicuous transitions and recapitulation, making the plot easy to follow even when it pauses for extended background information.

Dialogue dominates much of the story and is the chief instrument of characterization. Each speaker has a distinctive verbal register. Lawyers Higgins, Burch, and Judge Mackinnon speak briskly and comparatively plainly, while Mustard Bilton uses relaxed rural colloquialisms. Mrs. Mullarky’s speech is represented through an Irish-American stage dialect. Philo Gubb’s language is the strongest stylistic signature: he speaks in malformed, redundantly elaborate pseudo-professional English, using phrases such as “the present time and moment,” “disappeared away,” and “accompany yourself with me.” He mispronounces “detective” as “deteckative,” overuses formal legalistic constructions, and turns simple statements into pompous circumlocutions. His speech reflects both social aspiration and comic self-importance: he has absorbed the vocabulary of correspondence-school detection without mastering its idiom or methods.

Characterization is economical and caricatural but affectionate. Gubb is vain, literal-minded, ceremonious, and largely incompetent as a reasoner, yet he is also honest, diligent, polite, and kind. His inflated sense of professional dignity makes him ridiculous, but his willingness to help Dolly and his refusal to dismiss the loss of a dog give him warmth. O’Hara is characterized indirectly through anecdotes, his will, and the instructions he leaves behind; even after death, he effectively directs the action. The rival heirs are drawn as grasping and cantankerous, while Dolly functions as the story’s sincere emotional center. The supporting cast consists of sharply recognizable comic types: practical lawyers, a genial judge, a lazy loafer, and a mocking housekeeper.

The humor rests on incongruity, verbal distortion, dramatic irony, and parody. Gubb repeatedly interprets mockery as praise, treats elementary observations as advanced deduction, and behaves as though crawling into a dog-house were an act of formidable professional technique. The audience understands more than he does, especially when O’Hara’s instructions reveal that Gubb’s predictable habits have been built into the joke. The story also employs reversals in quick succession: the missing dog leads to the missing witness; the witness fails to resolve the double will; and a hidden third will settles everything. Gubb’s apparent success is therefore both real and comic. He finds the dog, the witness, and the valid will, but does so precisely because O’Hara anticipated his clumsy methods.

Structurally, the story interweaves several plot strands that converge neatly. The opening material about Gubb’s dubious investment and enormous fiancée supplies serial continuity and establishes his gullibility. The immediate mystery then begins with the search for Mustard, expands into the history of O’Hara and the two-sided will, and connects with Dolly’s missing dog. Exposition is substantial, but it is broken up by dialogue, jokes, and small discoveries. The climax arrives in two stages: first, Gubb discovers the envelope in the dog-house and finds both Waffles and Mustard; second, Mustard reveals that neither side of the disputed document is the final will. The closing line restores Gubb’s comic self-image by allowing him to attribute his success to a correspondence-course lesson.

The setting is a lightly sketched Midwestern town whose offices, courthouse culture, bridge, streets, and familiar local personalities create a communal, provincial atmosphere. Riverbank operates as a world where everyone knows everyone else’s business and a disputed will can become the town’s sole topic within hours. The social world is recognizable rather than realistic in depth, serving as a compact stage for eccentricity and farce. Period details—telegrams, handwritten wills, correspondence courses, side shows, cob pipes, and office blocks—reinforce the story’s historical character.

The overall tone is genial, satirical, and lightly sentimental rather than cynical. The story mocks pretension, greed, amateur expertise, and the conventions of scientific detection, but it rewards loyalty and affection. Its emotional material is deliberately simple: Dolly loves her uncle and her dog, while O’Hara’s final joke ultimately protects her inheritance. The resulting style can be described as deadpan comic narration enlivened by dialect dialogue, verbal malapropism, elaborate plotting, and affectionate parody of the amateur-detective genre.

# PHILO GUBB AND THE WILL ON BOTH SIDES

When Philo Gubb completed the paper-hanging of the three upper rooms of Judge Mackinnon’s residence, he received forty-eight dollars and sixty cents, cash in hand. The sixty cents represented two rolls of border which the Judge had purchased but which Mr. Gubb had not used. The forty-eight dollars represented labor, skill, paste, and the Judge’s desire to have Mr. Gubb out of the house before Mrs. Mackinnon decided to have the hall done also.

Mr. Gubb folded the money into his pocketbook and proceeded directly to the office of Mr. Jonas C. Lattimer, father of Syrilla Lattimer, whom Mr. Gubb hoped at some future time and occasion to marry.

Mr. Lattimer had sold Mr. Gubb one thousand shares of the Great Geyser Silver, Gold, Copper, Mica, Tin, and Natural Gas Consolidated Mining Company for five hundred dollars. The shares had originally been printed to sell for ten dollars each, but Mr. Lattimer had reduced them because he liked Mr. Gubb and because the printing on several of them was blurred.

The company owned a mine in Nevada. At least, it owned the rights to a hole in Nevada, and Mr. Lattimer had frequently assured Mr. Gubb that mineral wealth was bound to come out of that hole as soon as enough money had been put into it.

So far the process had been all put and no come.

Mr. Gubb had paid one hundred and seventy-five dollars on the stock. He now took twenty-five dollars from his pocketbook and laid it on Mr. Lattimer’s desk.

“I come to reduce down the present outstanding indebtedness,” he said, “so that when the mine becomes a dividend-paying proposition I will own the shares more completely than heretofore.”

Mr. Lattimer looked at the money with regret. He was always sorry to receive money on the mining stock, because every payment reduced the amount still due.

“You don’t want to strain yourself, Philo,” he said. “A man ought to keep a little ready cash.”

“I retain twenty-three dollars and sixty cents,” said Mr. Gubb. “The sixty cents is an emergency reserve.”

Mr. Lattimer pushed a cigar toward him.

“You heard from Syrilla lately?”

Mr. Gubb’s long face brightened. The effect was much like lighting one candle in an empty railway station, but it was an improvement.

“This present morning I received a telegraphic communication,” he said. “It was of a highly satisfactory nature.”

He drew the telegram from his coat and read it aloud:

> LOST SEVEN POUNDS THIS WEEK STOP PROFESSOR PULTZ SAYS IF THIS KEEPS UP CONTRACT ENDS BY OCTOBER STOP NOW EAT NO POTATOES CABBAGES TURNIPS PARSNIPS BEETS CARROTS ONIONS SQUASH PUMPKINS CUCUMBERS CORN TOMATOES OR PEAS STOP AM ALLOWED ONE RADISH SUNDAYS STOP LOVE SYRILLA

Syrilla Lattimer was, at the time, appearing with Pultz’s Colossal Congress of Living Wonders under the professional title of Princess Muscavado, the Mountain of Maidenly Magnificence. When Mr. Gubb had first become engaged to her, Syrilla weighed six hundred and twelve pounds. Professor Pultz had immediately placed her under contract, and the contract stated that she might leave the show when her weight fell below four hundred pounds.

Love gave Syrilla a reason for reducing, and Professor Pultz gave her a diet. Between them they had reduced her to four hundred and thirty-six pounds.

“Seven pounds!” said Mr. Lattimer. “That’s fine.”

“It is more than fine,” Mr. Gubb said. “It is hopeful. If Syrilla continues losing seven pounds per week, she will become free from the side-show bondage in a little more than five weeks. Naturally, I do not expect her to lose the entire seven pounds every week. A portion may be regained by the Sunday radish.”

“Could be,” said Mr. Lattimer.

Mr. Gubb replaced the telegram tenderly in his pocket. Having discharged a part of his debt and received news of his future bride’s continued decrease, he felt prepared to resume the practice of his other profession.

This profession was detective work.

Mr. Gubb was a graduate of the Rising Sun Correspondence School of Detection, Investigation, Shadowing, and the Complete Unmasking of Crime. He had completed Lessons One through Thirty-Seven, with the exception of Lesson Twenty-Two, which had been lost in the mail. He considered himself a paper-hanger by trade and a deteckative by intellectual preference.

His office occupied one room over the Riverbank Ice, Coal, and Feed Company. On the door he had painted:

> PHILO GUBB  
> INTERIOR DECORATOR  
> AND PRIVATE DETECKATIVE  
> STRICT CONFIDENCE USED

When he reached this office, he found Lawyer Higgins waiting outside.

Lawyer Higgins was a small, brisk man whose manner suggested that every minute had been entered on his time sheet and would be charged to somebody.

“Gubb,” he said, “I want you to find Mustard Bilton.”

Mr. Gubb unlocked the door.

“You have come to the correct place and location,” he said. “Kindly enter in.”

Lawyer Higgins entered, but he did not sit. Sitting, in his opinion, was something a man could do after winning a case.

“You know Mustard Bilton?” he asked.

“I know him by visual appearance and general reputation,” said Mr. Gubb. “He is an unemployed person who smokes a cob pipe and considers fishing a commercial occupation.”

“That’s the man. He has disappeared.”

“Disappeared away entirely?”

“He hasn’t been seen for nine days.”

Mr. Gubb sat behind his desk and put his fingertips together in the manner recommended by Lesson Six, “How to Impress the Client Before Learning What the Trouble Is.”

“Was there,” he asked, “any blood stains, blunt instruments, cries in the night, footprints leading toward water, mysterious women in veils, or portions of torn correspondence?”

“No.”

Mr. Gubb appeared disappointed but professional.

“Then the crime is unusually deep,” he said.

“It may not be a crime at all. Mustard is wanted as a witness in the O’Hara will matter.”

Mr. Gubb nodded. Everyone in Riverbank knew of the O’Hara will matter, but not everyone understood it. Those who understood it least explained it most frequently.

Haddon O’Hara had been Riverbank’s leading practical joker. He had never become wealthy enough to be called an eccentric during life, but when he died and left an estate valued at eighty thousand dollars, his jokes were remembered as eccentricities.

He had once sent each member of the town council an official-looking notice ordering him to report at the freight depot with a shovel. He had nailed a silver dollar to the courthouse steps. He had placed a sign reading FRESH PAINT on a bench that had not been painted for six years. He had entered a pig in the county baby parade under the name of Aloysius O’Hara, and the pig had received honorable mention because the judges were afraid it belonged to an influential family.

In spite of these habits, Haddon O’Hara was liked. His jokes were troublesome, but they were seldom cruel, and he laughed as readily when one was played on him.

Then he died.

He died and left a will.

More exactly, he left two wills, and this was the difficulty.

The wills were written on opposite sides of one sheet of heavy legal paper. One side left five hundred dollars to Dolly O’Hara, his orphaned niece; one hundred dollars to the Riverbank Home for Aged Horses; fifty dollars to Judge Mackinnon for “legal services never rendered and therefore worth the price”; and the entire remainder of the estate to Miss Ardelia Doblin.

The other side contained the same words, line for line, comma for comma, and flourish for flourish, except that the name Sarah Kinsey appeared where the name Ardelia Doblin appeared.

Both wills were dated April 17. Both were signed by Haddon O’Hara. Both were witnessed by Mustard Bilton and two men who had since died. The ink appeared equally old. The handwriting appeared equally shaky. Neither side bore a blot, thumbprint, grease spot, fold, or other mark by which it might be proved to have been written before the other.

If the Ardelia side had been written last, Ardelia inherited. If the Sarah side had been written last, Sarah inherited.

Miss Doblin and Miss Kinsey had disliked each other for twenty-two years. The disputed estate gave this dislike a financial foundation.

Lawyer Higgins represented Ardelia Doblin.

“I’ll pay you fifty dollars when you produce Mustard Bilton,” he told Gubb. “He witnessed both writings. He may know which one was last.”

“I comprehend the legal crisis,” said Mr. Gubb. “The final side written is the final will made.”

“Exactly.”

“And until Mustard is produced into court, Miss Doblin remains deprived of funds which may or may not rightfully belong to her, depending on what Mustard knows.”

“Exactly.”

“And you pay fifty dollars.”

“When he is found.”

Mr. Gubb arose and extended his hand.

“I accept the case under strict silence,” he said.

Lawyer Higgins had barely gone when Lawyer Burch entered.

Lawyer Burch represented Sarah Kinsey. He was a large, slow man who believed no statement should be made until it had been allowed to mature in the mind. His pauses often lasted long enough to become recesses.

“Gubb,” he said, and paused, “I wish you to find Mustard Bilton.”

Mr. Gubb considered the professional ethics involved. Lesson Eleven warned the student never to betray a client’s confidence. It did not warn him against accepting another client who wanted the same thing.

“You desire the same missing personage who is wanted elsewhere in certain legal circles?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“I am not at liberty to tell you whether I have been hired by another party, person, or lawyer,” said Gubb. “But if I was, it would be a confidence. Therefore I do not tell you I was.”

“Quite right,” said Lawyer Burch. “I will pay you fifty dollars to locate Bilton and bring him to my office.”

Mr. Gubb frowned.

“It may be impossible to bring one entire man to two separate law offices simultaneously at the same instant,” he said.

“Bring him to Judge Mackinnon’s office, then. Both sides can question him there.”

“That removes the ethical obstacle from the path,” said Gubb. “I accept.”

Lawyer Burch left, and Mr. Gubb took from a drawer a magnifying glass, a tape measure, a notebook, two small plaster boxes for preserving footprints, a pair of false whiskers, and the correspondence lesson entitled “Missing Men: Where They Go and Why They Should Not.”

He had just arranged these on his desk when there came a light knock.

The young woman who entered was Dolly O’Hara.

She was not beautiful in the aggressive manner of the actresses whose pictures were displayed in the drugstore window, but she had gentle eyes and the sort of face that made a man wish he had not said anything foolish during the previous five minutes. Mr. Gubb stood at once and brushed a shred of wallpaper from his sleeve.

“Mr. Gubb,” she said, “I’ve come about Waffles.”

Mr. Gubb looked toward the door.

“Is he waiting outside?”

“No. He’s gone.”

“Gone where?”

“If I knew that, he wouldn’t be lost.”

This was so exact that Mr. Gubb wrote it in his notebook.

“What is Waffles?” he asked.

“My dog.”

Mr. Gubb’s professional expression weakened slightly. A missing witness in an eighty-thousand-dollar will case was deteckative work of the first order. A missing dog was lower in the lessons, between “Unexplained Chicken Losses” and “The Anonymous Valentine.”

Dolly saw the change in his face.

“I know he’s only a dog,” she said. “But Uncle Haddon gave him to me. Waffles is almost the only thing of Uncle’s I expected to keep. I’m not going to get the estate, no matter which of those women wins it.”

Mr. Gubb immediately closed the lesson on missing men.

“A dog,” he said with dignity, “is no less missing because he travels on four legs. The Rising Sun course recognizes footprints regardless of quantity. When was Waffles last observed in a present condition?”

“Three nights ago. I put him in his house before I went to bed. In the morning the chain was unfastened and he was gone.”

“Was the chain broken?”

“No.”

“The collar?”

“Gone with him.”

“Did Waffles possess enemies?”

“He barked at Mrs. Mullarky.”

“Many persons do,” said Mr. Gubb.

Mrs. Mullarky had been Haddon O’Hara’s housekeeper and remained in Dolly’s service. She was considered a useful woman in the house and a dangerous woman in conversation.

“Did your late uncle have especial affection toward the dog?” Gubb asked.

“Oh, yes. He brought Waffles home as a puppy. He said Waffles was the only creature in Riverbank who understood his jokes, because Waffles never asked him to explain one.”

“A clue,” said Mr. Gubb.

“What is?”

“I cannot state until subsequent developments disclose whether it is one. Many clues do not become clues until after they are no longer needed.”

Dolly offered him two dollars.

Mr. Gubb looked at the money and then at her anxious face.

“The professional deteckative fee will be collected when the dog is found,” he said. “If he is not found, the fee is nothing, plus expenses.”

“What expenses?”

“None as yet.”

Mr. Gubb accompanied Dolly to the O’Hara house.

It was an old square house near the edge of town, with a porch that had settled in the middle as if tired of holding itself up. Waffles’s house stood in the rear yard beneath an elm. It was a substantial doghouse, shingled, painted green, and large enough to accommodate a dog, a child, or a private detective of unusually narrow construction.

Mrs. Mullarky met them at the back door.

“So this is the great detective man, is it?” she said. “Well, praise be, Dolly, we’ll have the dog back before supper, unless Mr. Gubb mistakes himself for a clue and follows his own legs home.”

Mr. Gubb accepted this as encouragement.

“You may joke, Mrs. Mullarky,” he said, “but the deteckative intellect is frequently hidden beneath an exterior surface that deceives the untrained observer.”

“Hidden deep, is it?” she asked.

“Extremely.”

“That I believe.”

Mr. Gubb began with the ground surrounding the doghouse. He knelt, measured three impressions, and made sketches of them. One was the heel mark of Dolly’s shoe. One was made by the milkman. The third proved, after prolonged examination, to be the place where Mrs. Mullarky had set down a flatiron to cool.

He examined the chain.

He examined the staple.

He examined the empty water pan and found water.

He scraped a stain from the door and placed it in a folded paper.

“What is that?” Dolly asked.

“Paint,” said Gubb. “But frequently paint is used by criminals to resemble paint.”

He then requested specimens of every brush, blanket, rug, and garment with which Waffles had recently come in contact. Dolly supplied a worn piece of carpet on which the dog had slept, his brush, and a blue woolen shawl she had sometimes thrown across him in cold weather.

Mr. Gubb carried these articles to his office.

For two days he subjected them to microscopic examination.

The Rising Sun Correspondence School had sold him the microscope as a special graduation accessory, although he had not graduated. It magnified objects with great vigor while leaving their meaning unchanged.

From the brush he obtained thirteen brown hairs, four gray hairs, one red hair, two human hairs, three carpet fibers, and a bristle that may have come from the brush.

From the carpet he obtained eleven brown hairs, a piece of cracker, sand, coal dust, lint, and the wing of a moth.

From the shawl he obtained blue wool, brown dog hair, white cotton, a strand of Dolly’s hair, and a flea.

Mr. Gubb arranged the discoveries in envelopes and labeled them Exhibit A through Exhibit H. He compared the brown hairs one with another. They all resembled brown dog hairs. He compared the sand with sand from the riverbank, from Main Street, and from the schoolyard. It resembled all three, as sand will.

At the end of the second day he had reached no conclusion, unless the flea led to the conclusion that Waffles had at some period been acquainted with fleas.

The inductive method had again failed Mr. Gubb, as it usually did. He therefore adopted the more reliable method of walking around town and asking questions.

He questioned the station agent, the freight agent, the express agent, the ferryman, two butchers, three boys, the chief of police, and a traveling umbrella-mender. None had seen Waffles. The boys claimed to have seen dogs of every description except the description Mr. Gubb gave. One of them offered to sell him a yellow dog for seventy-five cents.

Nor did these inquiries locate Mustard Bilton.

Mustard’s room over Kling’s harness shop had not been occupied for nine days. His fishing pole was gone, but his best coat remained. His landlady said he owed three weeks’ rent, but this supplied no information because Mustard had often remained visible while owing considerably more.

Mr. Gubb searched the riverbank. He searched the railway yards. He visited two barns, a smokehouse, and the abandoned brick kiln. He found a broken bottle, a horseshoe, three buttons, and a handkerchief marked “E. P.” None belonged to Mustard. One button, however, exactly matched a missing button on Mr. Gubb’s own vest.

Meanwhile Riverbank discussed the O’Hara wills.

Miss Ardelia Doblin declared that Haddon had always admired her.

Miss Sarah Kinsey declared that Haddon had always admired anyone he could tease.

Miss Doblin said Sarah had pursued Haddon shamelessly.

Miss Kinsey replied that nobody could pursue Haddon shamelessly because shame would be the only reason to pursue him.

Each woman was sixty or thereabouts, and each had been expecting to marry Haddon for twenty years. Haddon had encouraged both expectations just enough to keep them lively and had avoided marriage by the simpler process of not marrying either.

On the fourth morning Mr. Gubb received a visit from Judge Mackinnon.

“Any progress?” the Judge asked.

“Progress has been made in numerous directions,” said Gubb. “Unfortunately none has reached a destination.”

“Find Mustard?”

“Not in a located condition.”

“Find the dog?”

“Equally absent.”

The Judge smiled.

“Haddon O’Hara used to say you’d be the best detective in Iowa if criminals would only leave wallpaper paste on everything.”

Mr. Gubb bowed.

“I am obliged for the high compliment.”

“It wasn’t altogether— Never mind. Gubb, there’s something peculiar here. O’Hara dies. Mustard vanishes. Then Dolly’s dog vanishes. Haddon was fond of that dog, and Mustard witnessed both sides of the will.”

“I have connected all three facts mentally,” said Gubb.

“And?”

“They are all connected.”

“How?”

“That is what remains concealed.”

Judge Mackinnon looked about the office. On the desk lay a dog collar borrowed for comparative purposes, a lump of river mud, the three buttons, the microscope, and a photograph of Syrilla in her professional costume.

“Who is that?” he asked.

“My future bride previous to reducing,” said Mr. Gubb.

“Ah.”

“She is now considerably less.”

“Glad to hear it.”

Judge Mackinnon departed, and Mr. Gubb sat with his elbows on the desk. The Judge’s words had moved something in his mind, but not far enough for him to see what it was.

Haddon had been fond of Waffles.

Mustard had witnessed the wills.

Haddon had joked about everything.

The dog was gone.

Mustard was gone.

Mr. Gubb arose abruptly.

When the inductive method fails, Lesson Seventeen advised the student to return to the scene and inspect whatever he had neglected to inspect the first time. This, the lesson stated, was especially useful when the student had neglected almost everything.

Mr. Gubb returned to the O’Hara house.

Mrs. Mullarky was beating a rug on the clothesline.

“Back again, are ye?” she called. “Did the microscope tell ye the dog was brown?”

“It communicated several scientific indications,” said Mr. Gubb. “I am about to inspect the doghouse interiorly.”

“And did ye not do that before?”

“I inspected the vicinity, surrounding locality, chain, fastenings, earth, and exterior surface.”

“Meaning ye looked everywhere but where the dog lived.”

“The obvious,” said Mr. Gubb, “is generally overlooked because it is too plainly visible.”

“Ye overlooked it beautifully.”

He went to the doghouse and knelt before the entrance. The opening was low, but Mr. Gubb was thin and had the advantage of being shaped somewhat like a folded carpenter’s rule. He removed his coat, placed his hat on the grass, and entered headfirst.

The interior smelled of dog, dust, and old carpet. Mr. Gubb examined the floorboards. He examined the rear wall. He examined the side walls. Then, while turning, he struck his head against the roof.

The blow was not severe, but it caused him to observe that one board sounded hollow.

He tapped it again.

It still sounded hollow.

Mr. Gubb backed out, obtained a screwdriver from Mrs. Mullarky, and entered once more. Two screws held the board. When he removed them, the board dropped and struck him on the nose. Behind it was a narrow compartment, and within the compartment lay an envelope.

Across the envelope was written:

> TO PHILO GUBB, IF HE HAS SENSE ENOUGH TO LOOK HERE.

Mr. Gubb read this with satisfaction. The confidence of the late Haddon O’Hara in his professional abilities was touching.

He backed out of the doghouse with the envelope in his teeth.

Mrs. Mullarky stood with her hands on her hips.

“And what have ye fetched from the kennel?” she asked. “A bone?”

“A documentary clue,” said Mr. Gubb, brushing dust from his knees.

The envelope was sealed. Beneath Mr. Gubb’s name were the words:

> Open this when found. Follow directions exactly. Do not deliver the enclosed sealed paper until Waffles has been returned to Dolly.

Inside was a note and another envelope. The second envelope was heavy, sealed with red wax, and addressed to Judge Mackinnon, Executor of the Estate of Haddon O’Hara.

Mr. Gubb read the note:

> Dear Gubb:
>
> If you have reached this point, Dolly has hired you to find Waffles, as I expected she would. You have probably examined hairs through a microscope, measured footprints, and bothered half the town. That is why I allowed four days before the next step.
>
> Take the County Road west to the old Dempsey cattle shed beyond Miller’s Creek. Enter by the small rear door. Bring Dolly’s dog home. Bring anything else you find there. Then deliver the sealed envelope to Judge Mackinnon in the presence of the interested lawyers and claimants.
>
> Do not try to reason this out. You will only delay matters.
>
> HADDON O’HARA

Mr. Gubb read the note twice.

It was impressive evidence of O’Hara’s understanding of scientific detection. The dead man had predicted the microscope, the measurements, the questions, and even the necessary four days. Mr. Gubb did not regard the final sentence as insulting. To him it merely meant that speed was essential.

He placed the sealed envelope inside his shirt.

“Mrs. Mullarky,” he said, “inform Miss Dolly that professional developments have reached a climax. I go to recover her dog, together with anything else located in association with him.”

“Would that include your senses?” she asked.

“If found,” said Mr. Gubb gravely, “all related articles will be brought back.”

The old Dempsey cattle shed stood five miles west of Riverbank, beyond Miller’s Creek, in a pasture no longer used except by weeds. Mr. Gubb hired Alf Sproat’s delivery wagon for fifty cents and drove there.

The front doors of the shed sagged on rusty hinges. He went around to the rear and found the small door. From within came a bark.

“Waffles!” cried Mr. Gubb.

The bark became a series of joyful explosions.

Mr. Gubb opened the door. A brown dog rushed upon him, placed muddy paws on his shirt, knocked off his hat, and licked him across the mouth.

“Your identity is practically established,” said Mr. Gubb, when he could speak.

“Shut that door!” called a voice from the dimness. “He’ll run clean to town if you let him.”

On a pile of hay sat Mustard Bilton. He wore old trousers, a faded shirt, and an expression of complete comfort. Beside him were a fishing pole, a cob pipe, a sack of provisions, and seven empty sardine tins.

Mr. Gubb stared.

“Mustard Bilton!”

“That’s what folks mostly call me.”

“You are missing.”

“I ain’t missing to myself.”

“You have been sought for throughout Riverbank by two legal representatives, one private deteckative, various boys, and possibly the chief of police, although he did not appear greatly active.”

Mustard filled his pipe.

“I knowed you’d turn up,” he said. “Haddon said you would.”

Mr. Gubb drew himself erect.

“The process by which I have located you is confidential, but not accidental.”

“Found the letter in the doghouse, did you?”

“I did.”

“How long’d it take?”

“The exact duration is professionally immaterial.”

Mustard grinned.

“Haddon said four days. Said you’d spend two days looking at dog hair, one day asking everybody that didn’t know, and one day thinking. He allowed half a day either way.”

Mr. Gubb chose not to dispute the accuracy of this schedule.

“What are you doing here with the dog?”

“Waiting for you.”

“Why?”

“Because Haddon paid me to.”

Mustard struck a match on his shoe and lighted the pipe.

“A month before Haddon died,” he continued, “he come to me and says, ‘Mustard, I got a job that calls for a man with patience, no curiosity, and no regular employment.’ I says that sounds like me. He gives me fifty dollars then and promises fifty more from Judge Mackinnon after it’s over.

“He told me when he died I was to wait a week, then take Dolly’s dog out of his house at night and bring him here. He’d stocked the place with food for me and the dog. Said I was to stay till you come with a note from the kennel.”

“You stole Waffles?”

“Borrowed him. Haddon was particular about that. Said the dog had to go back in good condition. I been feeding him better than I feed myself.”

Waffles, who was eating from a pan, agreed with this by wagging his tail.

“And why did you disappear before the dog did?” asked Mr. Gubb.

“Haddon’s orders. He said the lawyers had to get worried enough to hire you. If the dog went first, you might hunt the dog without paying attention to me. If I went first and the dog followed, he said even you might connect us.”

Mr. Gubb felt the need to defend himself.

“I had already mentally connected both disappearances with the deceased party.”

“Sure,” said Mustard. “Haddon allowed you might.”

“You witnessed the two wills,” Gubb said sternly. “Do you know which side was written last?”

“I know,” said Mustard.

Mr. Gubb breathed deeply. Here was the secret for which Riverbank had argued, two women had quarreled, and two lawyers had offered fifty dollars each.

“Which?” he asked.

“Neither.”

Mr. Gubb looked at one wall of the shed and then at another.

“Both sides cannot be neither,” he said.

“They can if there’s a third will.”

Mr. Gubb’s hand went to the sealed envelope inside his shirt.

Mustard nodded.

“That’s it.”

The return to Riverbank was triumphal in everything except appearance. Mustard drove the wagon. Mr. Gubb sat beside him holding the sealed envelope. Waffles occupied the rear, where he barked at cows, fence posts, and one stump.

They stopped first at Dolly’s house.

Dolly came running from the porch when she heard Waffles bark. The dog leaped from the wagon and reached her in three bounds. She dropped to her knees and put both arms around him.

“Waffles! Oh, Waffles!”

The dog whined, licked her cheek, and attempted to climb entirely into her lap.

Mr. Gubb stood solemnly by. A private deteckative, he believed, should show no emotion at the successful conclusion of a case. He therefore looked at the elm tree until his eyes stopped watering.

Dolly rose and caught his hand.

“You found him!”

“I recovered him into your possession,” said Mr. Gubb. “He has suffered no apparent injury except association with Mustard Bilton.”

Mustard touched his hat.

“Dog’s fine, Miss Dolly.”

“I don’t care how you did it,” she said to Gubb. “I don’t care where he was. You brought him back.”

She tried to give Gubb the two dollars.

He took one.

“The other dollar is deducted,” he said, “because the case contained certain assistance furnished by the late Mr. O’Hara.”

Mrs. Mullarky looked into the wagon and saw Mustard.

“So ye found the loafer too!” she exclaimed.

“I was instructed to bring anything else discovered in the shed,” said Mr. Gubb.

“Did ye look for the shed?”

“I had no authority to remove real estate.”

Within half an hour Judge Mackinnon’s office was crowded.

Judge Mackinnon sat behind his desk. Lawyer Higgins and Miss Ardelia Doblin occupied one side of the room. Lawyer Burch and Miss Sarah Kinsey occupied the other. Dolly stood near the door with Waffles, who had been admitted because Haddon’s instructions seemed to make him an interested party.

Mustard Bilton leaned against the wall. Mr. Gubb stood in the center with the sealed envelope.

Miss Doblin was a tall, sharp woman dressed in black. Miss Kinsey was a shorter, rounder woman also dressed in black. Each wore mourning for Haddon, but neither had yet decided whether the mourning would be permanent or merely until she lost the estate.

“There he is!” cried Miss Doblin, pointing at Mustard. “Make him tell which will was last.”

“Yes,” said Miss Kinsey. “And make him tell the truth. Ardelia has probably promised him money.”

“I have done nothing of the kind!”

“You would if you thought of it.”

“Ladies,” said Judge Mackinnon, “we’ll proceed in order. Gubb, you located Mustard?”

“I did,” said Mr. Gubb.

“You also found Dolly’s dog?”

“The dog and the witness were simultaneously present in one abandoned agricultural structure.”

“Why?”

“Haddon told him to,” said Mustard.

Both women began talking at once. Judge Mackinnon struck his desk with a paperweight.

“Mustard,” he said, “tell us the whole thing.”

Mustard removed his cob pipe from his pocket. Judge Mackinnon pointed at it.

“Don’t light that.”

“I wasn’t figuring to. Just holds my hand steady.”

He told the story he had told Mr. Gubb. When he finished, Lawyer Higgins stepped forward.

“You admit witnessing both sides of the sheet?”

“Yep.”

“Which side was executed last?”

“The Ardelia side,” said Mustard.

Miss Doblin gave a cry of triumph. Miss Kinsey gave a cry of outrage.

Then Mustard added, “Unless it was the Sarah side.”

The cries reversed owners.

“What do you mean?” demanded Lawyer Burch.

“Well, Haddon wrote one side and signed it, and me and the other two witnessed. Then he turned the paper over and done the other. I can’t recollect which came first.”

“Then why did you say the Ardelia side?”

“I was thinking it might’ve been.”

“You just said you knew!” cried Miss Doblin.

“I know neither one was his last will.”

All eyes turned toward Mr. Gubb and the envelope.

Judge Mackinnon held out his hand.

Mr. Gubb did not surrender it.

“The written instructions specifically require delivery in the presence of the interested lawyers and claimants,” he said. “Are all present?”

“Everyone except Haddon,” said the Judge.

“He is represented by written documentary communication,” said Gubb, and handed over the envelope.

The red wax cracked under Judge Mackinnon’s thumb. Inside was a folded sheet and a smaller note.

The Judge unfolded the sheet first. He studied it. Then he looked at Dolly.

“This is a will,” he said.

Miss Doblin rose.

“Another will?”

“Dated June 3, two months after the double-sided document. Properly signed and witnessed. It revokes all former wills.”

“And who gets the estate?” Sarah Kinsey demanded.

Judge Mackinnon read:

> I, Haddon Patrick O’Hara, being sound in mind although frequently accused of the contrary, do declare this my final will. I give all property of every kind to my niece, Dolly O’Hara, except one hundred dollars to Mustard Bilton for services to be rendered, and twenty-five dollars each to Ardelia Doblin and Sarah Kinsey, on condition that each spend her twenty-five dollars on a gift for the other. I name Judge Mackinnon executor and direct him to pay all reasonable expenses caused by my final joke.

For several seconds nobody spoke.

Dolly stared at the Judge.

“I get—everything?”

“Everything except the amounts named.”

“But Uncle’s first wills only gave me five hundred dollars.”

“Those weren’t his final wills.”

“Then why did he make them?”

Judge Mackinnon opened the smaller note.

“I expect this explains.”

He read aloud:

> Dear Mackinnon:
>
> Ardelia and Sarah each spent twenty years trying to marry me for my money. It seems unfair that neither should get any return for the effort, so I have left each twenty-five dollars and the opportunity to improve her Christian disposition.
>
> Dolly never asked me for anything except to stop teasing people. She likes Waffles better than she likes money, which is why she should have both.
>
> I made the two-sided wills because one bad will causes ordinary trouble, while two bad wills on one sheet cause first-class trouble. I instructed Mustard to witness them and later arranged for him to disappear. I knew Higgins and Burch would hire Gubb. I also knew Dolly would hire Gubb when Waffles vanished. Gubb would eventually search the doghouse, provided nobody told him to begin there.
>
> Pay Gubb whatever rewards he has been promised. He will have earned them, although not in the way he thinks.
>
> If Ardelia and Sarah are still arguing, tell them I said the one who stops first was always my favorite.
>
> Yours deceasedly,  
> HADDON O’HARA

Miss Doblin stopped speaking.

Miss Kinsey also stopped.

Each then watched the other to see whether she would begin.

Lawyer Higgins drew Mr. Gubb aside and paid him fifty dollars. Lawyer Burch paid him another fifty. Dolly tried to pay him more, but he refused.

“One dollar was the agreed professional charge,” he said. “The additional reward is already sufficient to compensate the deteckative faculties.”

Judge Mackinnon paid Mustard his remaining fifty dollars. Mustard counted it twice and asked whether he was still required as a witness.

“Not unless the will is contested,” said the Judge.

“Anybody contesting?”

Miss Doblin looked at Miss Kinsey.

Miss Kinsey looked at Miss Doblin.

“No,” they said together.

Waffles, bored with legal procedure, put his front paws on Judge Mackinnon’s desk and seized Haddon’s explanatory note in his teeth.

“Drop that!” cried four people.

Dolly rescued it before he could eat more than one corner.

“He always did like Uncle’s jokes,” she said.

The next morning Philo Gubb returned to Mr. Lattimer’s office. From the hundred dollars paid by the lawyers, he placed fifty on the desk as an additional payment on the Great Geyser Silver, Gold, Copper, Mica, Tin, and Natural Gas Consolidated Mining Company stock.

“You’re doing well, Philo,” said Mr. Lattimer. “Found that missing witness, did you?”

“I found the witness, the dog, the final last will, and the rightful heiress.”

“That sounds like real detective work.”

“Deteckative work,” corrected Mr. Gubb.

“Did you reason it all out?”

Mr. Gubb considered the question. He thought of the microscope, the hairs, the sand, the flea, the questions, the doghouse, and the dead man’s note advising him not to reason.

“The solution,” he said at last, “was obtained by following the advanced principle contained in Lesson Seventeen of the Rising Sun Correspondence School course.”

“What principle is that?”

Mr. Gubb drew himself up with professional dignity.

“When everything else has failed,” he said, “look where you ought to have looked in the first place.”

# The Cartographer of Rain

In Bellweather, rain had always fallen in straight lines.

It came down neatly, silver threads from a gray sky, tapping roofs, rinsing windows, filling gutters. Children drew it as they saw it: a cloud, a row of vertical strokes, a black umbrella underneath.

Then, one Tuesday morning in April, the rain began to fall sideways.

It swept eastward through the town as if chased by an invisible broom. It slipped beneath doors, climbed staircases, and soaked only the left sleeves of coats. At the railway station, it entered the waiting room through a closed window and left through an open one without wetting the floor between. On Market Street, every raindrop curved around the statue of the town’s founder, leaving the bronze man perfectly dry while drenching all the pigeons at his feet.

By Wednesday, rain was rising from wells.

By Thursday, it fell upward from the river and vanished into the clouds.

By Friday, the people of Bellweather were frightened.

Only Mara Venn seemed pleased.

Mara lived in a narrow house behind the clockmaker’s shop, with her grandfather, Silas, and a white cat named Compass. She was seventeen, restless, and famous for drawing maps of places nobody needed mapped: the shortcut taken by ants across the bakery wall, the territory of shadows in the town square, the route followed by every lost button that rolled beneath the floorboards.

Silas called these drawings “impractical.”

Mara called them practice.

Her parents had been mapmakers too, though of a more respectable kind. When Mara was six, they had left Bellweather to chart the northern marshes. Their expedition never returned. Search parties found a broken lantern, three tent pegs, and one page torn from her mother’s notebook. On it was a single sentence:

The world is larger in bad weather.

Silas had hidden the page in a desk for years. Mara had found it anyway.

On Friday afternoon, while townspeople hammered boards over their windows, Mara stood in the garden with charcoal and paper. Rain spiraled around her in a slow corkscrew. Compass sat beneath a rosebush, dry and offended.

Mara watched the drops closely.

They did not move at random. They bent left above the chimney, circled twice around the pear tree, divided at the stone wall, and joined again over the alley.

“It’s a road,” she whispered.

“What is?” asked Silas from the doorway.

“The rain.”

“The rain is water.”

“So is a river. Rivers go somewhere.”

Silas tightened his dressing gown. He had been a tall man once, but grief and age had folded him inward. “Come inside before you catch your death.”

Mara did not move. She drew faster.

The rain made a path across the garden, over the wall, between the bakery and the clockmaker’s shop, then vanished into a patch of empty air at the end of Candle Lane.

No, not empty, Mara realized. Thin.

Some places in the world felt thin, as if distance had been stretched too tightly over them. Her mother had written about such places in the margins of atlases.

Mara rolled up her map.

“I know where it goes.”

Silas looked at her in alarm. “That is exactly the sort of sentence your mother used to say before something exploded.”

“She usually came back.”

“Until she didn’t.”

The words fell between them, heavier than rain.

Mara lowered her eyes. “I have to look.”

“No.”

“I may be the only person who can.”

“No.”

“What if this is connected to the marshes?”

Silas turned away.

Mara regretted saying it, but not enough to take it back. For eleven years, Bellweather had spoken of her parents in softened phrases. A tragic disappearance. A brave expedition. A terrible uncertainty. Mara hated the uncertainty most. It had no shape, no edge, no place on a map.

Silas closed the door.

By midnight, the storm had grown stranger. Rain drummed beneath the roof tiles. Puddles crawled uphill. Water traced words across windows, though nobody could read the language.

Mara waited until the grandfather clock struck one. She packed bread, matches, string, charcoal, three pencils, her mother’s torn notebook page, and a brass compass that had never pointed north. The cat Compass tried to climb into her bag.

“Not this time,” she whispered, lifting him out.

He climbed in again.

Mara sighed. “Fine.”

She left a note for Silas and slipped into the storm.

Candle Lane was deserted. The rain flowed along it like a shining herd, all drops moving toward the brick wall at the end. Mara followed.

The wall belonged to an abandoned soap factory. She knew every crack in its surface. As a child, she had drawn each brick. Yet tonight, between the seventy-third and seventy-fourth bricks from the ground, a gap had appeared.

It was no wider than a needle.

Rain streamed into it.

Mara placed her palm against the wall. The bricks felt soft and cold, like clay beneath a river. She pushed. Her hand went through.

Then the wall opened.

Beyond it lay not the ruined factory yard but a vast blue country under a sky of moving water.

Mara stepped forward.

For a moment she fell sideways. Rain rushed past her ears. The world twisted, and the ground arrived unexpectedly beneath her boots.

She stood on a road made of dark glass. It curved through blue grass toward a forest where drops hung motionless among the trees. Above, rivers crossed the sky, winding through clouds like silver veins.

Compass climbed out of the bag and sneezed.

“Well,” Mara said. “Mother was right.”

She turned to mark the doorway, but the brick wall had disappeared. Behind her stretched miles of glass road.

Mara’s heart lurched. She took a breath, then another.

“First rule of mapmaking,” she told Compass. “Never panic until you’ve recorded where you are.”

She drew the road, the forest, and three rivers in the sky. Her brass compass pointed ahead, trembling.

They walked.

The blue grass chimed against Mara’s boots. Occasionally, a drop of rain rose from the ground and floated upward. Within each drop, she saw a tiny reflection—not of herself, but of Bellweather. A woman lit a stove. A boy searched for a missing shoe. Silas stood in Mara’s bedroom, holding her note.

She looked away.

At the forest’s edge stood a wooden sign:

ALL LOST WEATHER MUST BE DECLARED.

Beneath it sat a man in a yellow coat behind a small desk. He had a long nose, damp hair, and spectacles speckled with rain. A teapot steamed beside his elbow.

“Name?” he asked.

“Mara Venn.”

“Place of origin?”

“Bellweather.”

“Purpose of visit?”

“Your rain is leaking into my town.”

The man sighed and opened an enormous ledger. “It isn’t our rain.”

“It came through here.”

“Many things come through here. Few belong here.” He dipped his pen into the teapot instead of the ink bottle and wrote with tea. “Do you have an appointment with the Custodian?”

“No.”

“Invitation?”

“No.”

“Prophecy?”

“Not that I know of.”

“Dead ancestor with unfinished business?”

“My parents disappeared eleven years ago.”

The man paused.

“What were their names?”

“Elian and Sera Venn.”

His chair creaked as he leaned back. “Ah.”

Mara gripped the edge of the desk. “You know them?”

“I knew of them.”

“Where are they?”

He removed his spectacles and polished them slowly. “Maps are dangerous here, Miss Venn.”

“So are unhelpful men behind desks.”

Compass hissed in agreement.

The man glanced at the cat. “Follow the glass road until it becomes a staircase. At the top, you’ll find the House of Storms. Ask for the Custodian. Do not leave the road, do not drink from the sky, and if you hear someone calling your name from inside a puddle, be polite but do not answer.”

“Why?”

“Because whatever is calling will learn your voice.”

Mara wrote down the warning.

“One more thing,” he said. “If you find what you came for, it may not be what you wanted.”

“That sounds like a prophecy.”

“No. Just experience.”

The road wound deeper into the forest. Rain hung everywhere, suspended like crystal beads. When Mara touched one, thunder murmured in the distance.

After an hour, the glass beneath her feet rose in shallow steps. The forest fell away. Mara climbed into the sky.

At the summit stood a black house balanced on the edge of a cloud.

It was enormous and crooked, with chimneys shaped like trumpets and windows flashing with lightning. Rain poured from its gutters in every direction: down into the land, up into the rivers overhead, and sideways toward doors that opened onto places Mara could not see.

She knocked.

A woman with silver eyes answered. Her hair moved around her face as though stirred by a constant wind.

“Mara Venn,” she said.

Mara stiffened. “How do you know my name?”

“Your parents talked about you.”

The woman stepped aside.

Mara entered.

The House of Storms contained a thousand rooms and, somehow, no walls. Snow fell over one carpet. A desert wind blew across another. Thunder slept curled beside a fireplace, rumbling softly. Shelves rose into darkness, crowded with jars labeled FIRST FROST, UNSHED TEARS, MONSOON—HANDLE WITH CARE, and THE LAST FOG OF A FORGOTTEN ISLAND.

The silver-eyed woman moved through it all without getting wet.

“I am Aster Vale,” she said, “Custodian of Unfinished Weather.”

“Where are my parents?”

Aster studied her. “Direct as a lightning strike. You have your mother’s manners.”

“Are they alive?”

“Yes.”

The answer was so simple that Mara did not understand it at first.

Alive.

The word opened inside her like a door.

“Take me to them.”

Aster’s expression held no joy. “Your parents came here while mapping the northern marshes. They discovered a breach—a place where the weather between worlds had begun to mix. They crossed over to close it.”

“They succeeded?”

“For a time.”

Aster led Mara past a staircase made of hailstones. “Every world has weather, but weather is more than wind and water. It carries memory. Mood. Possibility. A storm from one world can alter another. A rain of forgetting may erase a city. A wind of longing may send an entire population walking west. The barriers must be maintained.”

“And now one is breaking over Bellweather.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because your parents stopped repairing it.”

They arrived at a round door. Aster placed her hand against it.

Beyond lay a circular chamber filled with maps.

They covered the walls, the floor, and the domed ceiling. Some were painted on paper. Others were etched into metal, woven from thread, or formed from tiny clouds. At the center of the room, beneath a column of rain, stood Elian and Sera Venn.

They had not aged.

Mara recognized them instantly. Her father’s dark curls. Her mother’s sharp chin. The green coat Sera had worn on the morning they left.

They stood side by side, drawing on a map suspended in the air.

“Mother?” Mara said.

Sera’s pencil stopped.

She turned.

The pencil fell from her hand.

“Mara?”

Her father looked up. His face broke open with wonder and pain. They crossed the room together and pulled Mara into their arms.

For a while, there was no room, no storm, no missing years. Mara smelled lamp oil on her father’s coat and peppermint on her mother’s breath. She felt six years old, lifted between them as they laughed.

Then she felt the unchanged smoothness of their faces.

She stepped back.

“Eleven years,” she said.

Her father’s smile faded. “Here, it has been eleven months.”

Mara’s joy sharpened into anger. “You could have come home.”

“We tried,” Sera said.

“For eleven months?”

“The breach trapped us. Whenever we opened a path to Bellweather, unstable weather escaped through it. We believed we could finish the repairs.”

“You left me.”

“We thought we’d return before winter.”

“You left Grandfather.”

Elian reached for her, but Mara moved away.

Around them, maps shivered in the windless chamber. The central column of rain had begun to bend eastward.

Aster watched from the door. “The breach is widening.”

Sera turned to the floating map. “We’ve lost the western seam.”

A crack appeared across the map, bright as lightning. At once, rain burst from the ceiling and swept sideways through the chamber.

Aster raised both hands. The drops froze in place.

“For years in Bellweather,” she said, “and months here, your parents have tried to preserve both the passage and the barrier. It cannot be done. The breach must be sealed completely.”

Elian looked at Mara.

She understood before he spoke.

“If we seal it,” he said, “the road home disappears.”

“Then come with me now.”

“The storm would follow,” Sera said. “Not only rain. All of this.”

She gestured toward the maps. Mara saw lines connecting Bellweather to whirlwinds, blizzards, red clouds, and oceans that floated upside down.

“What happens if the breach stays open?” Mara asked.

“Your town becomes the first crossing point,” Aster replied. “Then the borders fail elsewhere. Eventually, there will be no distinction between climates, places, or worlds.”

“And if we close it?”

“Bellweather is safe. Your parents remain here.”

Mara stared at them.

It was crueler than uncertainty. For eleven years she had imagined their death, their rescue, their sudden return. Never had she imagined finding them exactly as they were and being asked to leave them behind.

“There must be another path,” she said.

Her parents exchanged a glance.

Mara knew that glance. They had used it over breakfast when she proposed mapping the inside of the chimney.

“What?”

Sera picked up her pencil. “There may be another way, but we cannot see it.”

“Show me.”

They led her to the largest map on the floor. It depicted the breach as a black circle surrounded by thousands of fine lines. Most were tangled beyond recognition.

“We mapped every path the storm takes,” Elian said. “All lead through the breach.”

Mara knelt.

The map was beautiful, precise, and useless.

“You drew the rain,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You drew where it comes from and where it goes.”

“Yes.”

“But you didn’t draw where it refuses to go.”

Her parents were silent.

Mara remembered the statue in Market Street, dry amid soaked pigeons. The rain curving around the pear tree. Water entering a waiting room without touching its floor.

She pulled out her charcoal.

“Every road is shaped by the places it avoids.”

She began marking the empty spaces between the lines.

At first, they seemed random. Then a pattern emerged: dry islands forming a spiral from the House of Storms to the glass road, from the road to Candle Lane, from Candle Lane beneath Bellweather, where they joined under the statue in Market Street.

Her mother knelt beside her. “A second boundary.”

“Not a boundary,” Mara said. “A drain.”

Aster’s silver eyes widened. “The founder’s statue.”

“What about it?”

“Bellweather’s founder was Orrin Vale. My brother. He crossed from this world three centuries ago and built the town around the anchor he used to close his passage.”

“The statue stands over it,” Mara said.

“If the anchor still holds, the excess weather can be drawn back through the old channel while the breach is sealed.”

“And my parents?”

Aster looked at the map.

“They would have one chance to cross.”

The room erupted into motion.

Elian and Sera drew the channel. Aster opened jars from the shelves and poured winds into the map. Mara charted the dry path while Compass chased sparks of lightning under a table.

The crack widened.

The House of Storms groaned. Doors flew open, revealing burning rain, black snow, and clouds filled with whispering faces. Thunder woke by the fireplace and began to roar.

“Now!” Aster shouted.

She struck the map with both palms.

The world folded.

Mara was running down the glass staircase with her parents behind her. Storms poured after them. The forest bent beneath a wind that smelled of salt and smoke. Rain called Mara’s name from every puddle.

“Mara,” it said in Silas’s voice.

“Mara,” it cried in her mother’s voice, though Sera was beside her.

She did not answer.

At the forest’s edge, the man in the yellow coat stood on his desk, waving a teapot.

“Passage closes in two minutes!” he called. “Possibly three! Time is metaphorical!”

The glass road shattered behind them.

Ahead, the blue world narrowed into a brick-shaped slit.

Mara jumped through.

She landed in Candle Lane under ordinary, downward-falling rain.

Her father tumbled after her. Then Compass. Sera was halfway through when the opening snapped inward, catching the edge of her green coat.

Elian grabbed her hands.

Mara grabbed Elian.

For one terrible second, the wall pulled back.

Then the cloth tore.

They fell together onto the cobblestones.

The slit vanished.

Beneath their feet, the ground trembled. Water rushed through the gutters toward Market Street. They followed it.

The town square had flooded. Rain circled the founder’s statue in a shining whirlpool. Windows glowed as frightened people watched from their homes.

Silas stood alone in the water, wearing boots and his dressing gown.

When he saw Mara, fury crossed his face first.

Then he saw the two figures behind her.

He became very still.

Sera stepped forward. “Father.”

Silas made a sound like a door opening in an abandoned house.

They embraced beneath the statue while rain spun around them.

“Anchor!” Mara shouted.

At the statue’s base, beneath the bronze pigeons, she found a small metal plate engraved with the same spiral she had drawn in the House of Storms. There was a keyhole in its center.

Elian searched his pockets. Sera searched hers.

“The key was in our field case,” she said. “We lost it in the marsh.”

The whirlpool rose to Mara’s knees.

Her brass compass jerked in her hand.

It had never pointed north.

Now it pointed to the keyhole.

Mara understood. The compass had belonged to her mother, and before that to Orrin Vale. It was not a compass at all.

She pressed its needle against the keyhole and turned.

The statue rang like a bell.

The whirlpool collapsed.

Every drop of strange rain in Bellweather lifted at once. Water streamed from roofs, cellars, coats, and chimneys. It rose into a twisting silver column above the statue. For an instant, Mara saw the blue forest inside it and Aster standing beside the black house, one hand raised in farewell.

Then the column narrowed to a thread.

The thread snapped.

Rain fell straight down.

By morning, the storm had passed.

The official explanation involved unusual winds, damaged pipes, and collective nervous exhaustion. Nobody believed it, but Bellweather had long understood that an unbelievable explanation was often more comfortable than the truth.

Elian and Sera returned to their narrow house behind the clockmaker’s shop. They had aged only eleven months, while Silas had aged eleven years. This was awkward at first. Silas alternated between embracing them and shouting at them. Sometimes he did both together.

Compass refused to leave Mara’s bag for a week.

As for Mara, she was given a room above the town archive and the title of Municipal Cartographer, though the mayor admitted he did not know what she was supposed to map.

“Everything important,” she told him.

She began with the places where rain did not fall.

Over the years, her collection grew. She mapped doors that appeared only in fog, roads that shortened when travelers told the truth, and a hill where lost voices gathered at sunset. She charted ordinary rivers too, and property lines, and the safest route from the schoolhouse to the bakery.

Her parents sometimes helped, though they had become cautious.

Silas called this improvement.

Every April, on the anniversary of the sideways rain, Mara walked to the end of Candle Lane and placed her hand against the wall. Usually it was only brick.

But once, many years later, when she was old enough to have silver in her hair, she felt something cold and soft beneath her palm.

A needle-thin gap appeared.

Through it came the scent of blue grass and distant thunder.

Mara smiled.

Then she took a piece of charcoal from her pocket and began to draw.
